# Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making

Kaitao Chen    Mianxin Liu\Corresponding    Daoming Zong    Chaoyue Ding
   Shaohao Rui    Yankai Jiang    Mu Zhou\Corresponding    Xiaosong Wang

###### Abstract

Complex medical decision-making involves cooperative workflows operated
by different clinicians. Designing AI multi-agent systems can expedite
and augment human-level clinical decision-making. Existing multi-agent
researches primarily focus on language-only tasks, yet their extension
to multimodal scenarios remains challenging. A blind combination of
diverse vision-language models (VLMs) can amplify an erroneous outcome
interpretation. VLMs in general are less capable in instruction
following and importantly self-reflection, compared to large language
models (LLMs) of comparable sizes. This disparity largely constrains
VLMs’ ability in cooperative workflows. In this study, we propose
MedOrch, a mediator-guided multi-agent collaboration framework for
medical multimodal decision-making. MedOrch employs an LLM-based
mediator agent that enables multiple VLM-based expert agents to exchange
and reflect on their outputs towards collaboration. We utilize multiple
open-source general-purpose and domain-specific VLMs instead of costly
GPT-series models, revealing the strength of heterogeneous models. We
show that the collaboration within distinct VLM-based agents can surpass
the capabilities of any individual agent. We validate our approach on
five medical vision question answering benchmarks, demonstrating
superior collaboration performance without model training. Our findings
underscore the value of mediator-guided multi-agent collaboration in
advancing medical multimodal intelligence.

## 1 Introduction

Complex clinical decision-making hinges on a comprehensive cognitive
ability from medical vision, language, and domain knowledge derived from
human experts. Using large language models (LLMs) alone can only support
language-level assessment ([Thirunavukarasu et al. 2023](#bib.bib34);
[Singhal et al. 2023](#bib.bib31)). The exploration of vision-language
models (VLMs) opens the possibility to clinical multimodal
decision-making driven by model advances ([Wu et al. 2023a](#bib.bib39);
[Li et al. 2023a](#bib.bib20); [Chen et al. 2024](#bib.bib6)).
Incorporating a joint strength of these models can enable a
collaborative framework to understand and inform high-quality
decision-making.

Emerging multi-agent systems have garnered increasing attention for
enhancing clinical decision-making ([Zhang et al. 2024c](#bib.bib46);
[Zhang et al. 2024a](#bib.bib43)). In contrast to a single agent, a
multi-agent system supports collaboration among different agents. Akin
to the real-world clinical workflow to glean various diagnostic
opinions, multi-agent systems can mirror the patient-care coordination
from diverse perspectives ([Basit et al. 2024](#bib.bib4)).

A multi-agent system often follows a voting or judging-based strategy
([Wang et al. 2022](#bib.bib37)), allowing multiple agents to contribute
to the decision-making process. To promote a deep interaction, it is
intuitive to establish competitive or collaborative agent roles ([Wang
et al. 2024](#bib.bib36); [Li et al. 2023b](#bib.bib21)). Collaborative
frameworks from Mixture of Agents (MoA) ([Wang et al.
2024](#bib.bib36)), CAMEL ([Li et al. 2023b](#bib.bib21)), and
ProAgent ([Zhang et al. 2024a](#bib.bib43)) highlight the model’s
cognitive preference to reveal complex cooperative reasoning. In
medicine, Multi-expert Prompting ([Long et al. 2024](#bib.bib27)) and
MedAgents ([Tang et al. 2023](#bib.bib33)) are examples for building a
role-playing multi-agent framework. However, these multi-agent systems
are largely restricted in handling language-only tasks. Although
MDagents ([Kim et al. 2024](#bib.bib16)) seeks a multimodal question
answering, it uses the GPT-4V for the small-scale experiment on vision
question answering (VQA) datasets (e.g., 50 samples per dataset) due to
the prohibitive cost. Meanwhile, several open-source medical VLMs have
begun outperforming general-purpose counterparts like GPT-4o in medical
VQA ([Bansal et al. 2024](#bib.bib3)), motivating us to design a
multi-VLM-agent system based on open-source models without API cost.
This raises an intriguing question: Can open-source multimodal agents
with heterogeneous abilities develop effective collaboration strategies
for clinical decision-making?

Realistic barriers emerge in constructing diverse agents and their
collaboration when building a multimodal decision-making system.
General-purpose models provide broad knowledge coverage, while
domain-specific models excel in capturing nuances in specialized
scenarios. A blind combination of these models can generate erroneous
interpretations and propagate via agent interactions. In addition, VLM’s
instruction following and importantly self-reflection capabilities
remain inferior to those of LLMs in similar sizes ([Zuo et al.
2025](#bib.bib47)). This remarkable gap limits the ability of VLMs to
engage in meaningful reflection, an essential capability in the progress
of multi-agent collaboration. Given the heterogeneous nature and
remarkable difference in capability of VLM agents, it becomes further
challenging to coordinate their interactions effectively.

We draw inspiration from social theory, where Socratic questioning
([Elder and Paul 1998](#bib.bib12)) fosters disciplined and reflective
dialogue through a sequence of structured questions. Such an approach
encourages critical reflection, evidence scrutiny, and clarification of
conceptual ambiguities ([Carey and Mullan 2004](#bib.bib5)). Translating
this insight to AI collaboration, we propose MedOrch, a mediator-guided
multi-agent collaboration framework. MedOrch incorporates a dedicated
LLM-based mediator agent that orchestrates the interaction and
reflection among multiple VLM-based expert agents to support
collaborative medical decision-making. Specifically, we construct the
VLM-based expert agents using open-source general-purpose and
domain-specific VLMs, leveraging their complementary strengths, rather
than using cost-prohibitive GPT-series models. To start, in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making"),
multiple VLM-based expert agents first generate responses to a given
question. The mediator agent then synthesizes the information and
formulates Socratic questions to prompt deeper reasoning from the
VLM-based expert agent. Next, relevant VLM-based expert agents rethink
and generate their responses based on the question of the mediator
agent. Finally, a judge agent integrates dialogues and provides a final
judgment to support medical decision-making.

The main contributions of this study are: (i) We propose MedOrch as a
novel multi-agent collaboration for improved medical decision-making. We
design the mediator agent to guide the interaction of open-source
VLM-based expert agents. (ii) Our design emphasizes joint abilities
gained from distinct open-source general-purpose and domain-specific
VLMs to enable multimodal decision-making without prohibitive API cost.
It is noteworthy that our multi-agent system outperforms the best of
multiple single-agent models, even in the presence of misleading inputs
from certain agents. (iii) We conduct comprehensive evaluations on five
benchmarks. Our approach achieves strong performance, demonstrating its
potential efficiency in medical multimodal scenarios.

![Refer to caption](2508.05996v2/framework801.png)

Figure 1: The mediator-guided multi-agent collaboration framework for
medical VQA. In the initial stage, multiple VLM expert agents
independently generate preliminary answers to a given question. To
promote deeper interaction, the mediator agent synthesizes the
information and formulates Socratic questions for expert agents.
Subsequently, the relevant expert agents reflect on the question and
generate refined responses accordingly. Finally, a judge agent analyzes
the dialogues between the mediator and expert agents and achieves a
systematic output.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Multi-Agent AI System

While LLMs as individual agents ([Yang et al. 2024](#bib.bib42);
[Grattafiori et al. 2024](#bib.bib13)) reveal language understanding,
evident challenges persist in complex reasoning, interpretation, and
decision-making ([Luo et al. 2025](#bib.bib28); [Cheng et al.
2024](#bib.bib9)). As a natural progression, building a multi-agent
system requires us to cultivate collective intelligence through
mechanisms of cooperation or competition ([Kim et al. 2024](#bib.bib16);
[Wang et al. 2024](#bib.bib36); [Du et al. 2023](#bib.bib11); [Zhang
et al. 2024a](#bib.bib43)).

Cooperative learning fosters the collective knowledge sharing and joint
decision-making via agent voting ([Wang et al. 2022](#bib.bib37)),
interdisciplinary collaboration ([Kim et al. 2024](#bib.bib16)), and
group discussions ([Chen, Saha, and Bansal 2023](#bib.bib7)). For
instance, ProAgent ([Zhang et al. 2024a](#bib.bib43)) is a multi-agent
reinforcement learning framework leveraging policy sharing and
inter-agent communication. Similarly, CORY ([Ma et al.
2024](#bib.bib29)) emulated human reflective group learning by
implementing cycles of proposal, negotiation, reflection, and revision
in programming and mathematical tasks. CAMEL ([Li et al.
2023b](#bib.bib21)) adopted a role-playing collaborative framework to
allow autonomous dialogue and multi-step coordination among agents, yet
it falls into role confusion and instruction redundancy. In the
meantime, competitive approach stimulates reasoning and creativity
through conflict, adversarial interactions, and debate ([Du et al.
2023](#bib.bib11); [Liang et al. 2023](#bib.bib23)). The Multi-Agent
Debate framework ([Du et al. 2023](#bib.bib11)) mitigates the
overconfidence in LLMs by introducing viewpoint conflict to promote
deeper reasoning. Similarly, MAD ([Liang et al. 2023](#bib.bib23))
integrates diverse perspectives through iterative critique and revision
to enhance mathematical reasoning and factual verification. MoA ([Wang
et al. 2024](#bib.bib36)) introduces a multi-agent collaboration by
organizing LLMs into a hierarchical architecture in language-only tasks.
However, extending MoA into multimodal scenarios is problematic, since
VLMs may amplify misinterpretations from other agents, ultimately
hindering the effectiveness of the collaborative workflow ([Kim et al.
2024](#bib.bib16)).

### 2.2 Multi-Agent in Healthcare

Multi-agent systems in healthcare can be used to advance clinical
knowledge sharing and workflow automation ([Zhang et al.
2024c](#bib.bib46)). Emerging efforts have focused on (a) role
configuration ([Long et al. 2024](#bib.bib27); [Chen et al.
2025](#bib.bib8); [Pandey, Amod et al. 2024](#bib.bib30)), (b) task
decomposition ([Sun et al. 2024](#bib.bib32); [Basit et al.
2024](#bib.bib4)), and (c) workflow simulation ([Wei et al.
2024](#bib.bib38); [Li et al. 2024](#bib.bib22)). First, role
configuration starts with multi-expert prompting ([Long et al.
2024](#bib.bib27)) to generate expert roles in a zero-shot manner.
MDTeamGPT ([Chen et al. 2025](#bib.bib8)) develops a multi-agent system
for multidisciplinary medical consultations, incorporating a primary
physician mechanism and a residual discussion structure. Second, task
decomposition utilizes multiple role-playing agents to improve the task
performance. For instance, PathGen ([Sun et al. 2024](#bib.bib32))
enhances the quality of pathological captions through role-based agents.
MEDAID ([Basit et al. 2024](#bib.bib4)) decomposes complex medical
queries through query rewriting and context encoders. Third, workflow
simulation frameworks are designed to mimic insights in clinical
environments. MEDCO ([Wei et al. 2024](#bib.bib38)) simulates the
collaboration of patients, medical experts, and doctors, providing
personalized and precise clinical case training. In addition, agent
hospital ([Li et al. 2024](#bib.bib22)) simulates a hospital system that
integrates domain-specific knowledge bases to automate data generation
and address specific tasks.

The above multi-agent studies are primarily driven by single-modal and
close-source LLMs. Multi-agent systems remain largely underexplored in
multimodal decision-making scenarios, especially under the capacity of
open-source models. Although MDagents ([Kim et al. 2024](#bib.bib16))
leverages the multi-agent to address medical VQA tasks, its reliance on
a limited-scale experiment (only 50 samples per dataset) and the high
cost of GPT-4V significantly restricts its clinical applicability. In
contrast, our study focuses on complex medical multimodal scenarios by
integrating different open-source vision-language and language-only
models, as well as by combining general-purpose and domain-specific
models, to enable practical clinical multimodal decision-making.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Overview

MedOrch aims to enhance the multi-agent collaborative performance of
medical VQA tasks. The proposed system introduces three key agent
categories: expert agents, a mediator agent, and a judge agent, as shown
in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making").
Expert agents are responsible for answering visual-language questions.
The mediator agent is our key design, which synthesizes opinions,
resolves conflicts, and facilitates discussions. The judge agent
conducts the summarization and makes the final decision. The mediator
agent and judge agent are driven by specific prompts. See Appendix
Section Prompts for more details.

### 3.2 Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration

#### I. Initial VQA Stage.

Upon receiving a medical question, multiple expert agents generate
preliminary responses in parallel. Each agent then independently reasons
through the question and forms a response, contributing to a diverse set
of initial opinions. Initial opinions consist of the question analysis
and answer options.

#### II. Multi-Agent Collaboration.

The mediator agent plays a central role in guiding the communication
among expert agents. Its core responsibilities include analyzing the
viewpoints from multiple expert agents, identifying opinion conflicts,
and driving additional rounds of necessary discussions.

Analysis of expert agent’s answer. The mediator agent first
systematically compares the initial responses from all expert agents. It
identifies areas of consensus and disagreement, and flags responses that
exhibit logical inconsistencies or semantic ambiguities, thereby laying
the foundation for targeted follow-up discussion.

Decision on whether additional discussion is needed. Based on the
comparative analysis, the mediator agent determines whether an
additional dialogue with expert agents is required. If no significant
discrepancies are identified, the decision is marked as “No”.
Conversely, if critical issues arise or unclear reasoning are detected,
it initiates a focused dialogue with the relevant expert agents to
resolve these concerns, and the decision is recorded as “Yes”.

Socratic questioning. Once it is determined that further discussion is
needed, the mediator agent engages in structured Socratic dialogues with
the expert agents. The dialogues aim to promote information
clarification, disaggregate reasoning, and resolve core disagreements.
Each round of dialogue follows a well-defined format, including: Opening
the statement. The mediator agent begins by asserting itself prompted as
“the final authority on medical decisions” responsible for summarizing,
reviewing, and synthesizing the opinions of all agents who act as
experts. Summary of other agents. To facilitate information sharing and
encourage collaboration, the mediator agent summarizes the viewpoints of
other agents and highlights points of disagreement with the current
agent’s position. Review of the current agent. The mediator agent
reviews the core conclusions of the current agent, e.g., “You mentioned
…” and presents the reasoning behind their argument. Analysis and
questioning. Finally, the mediator agent raises in-depth questions
targeting the main points of contention, ensuring the inquiry remains
focused on substantial conflicts rather than vague or broad questions.

Feedback-based answering. Upon receiving the instruction from the
mediator agent, the relevant expert agents reconstruct their initial
answers based on the question. This becomes an evolutionary process that
involves reinterpreting the original image content, correcting logical
errors, and clarifying inconsistencies. Through this refinement, the
overall quality, coherence, and explanatory depth of the final responses
are evidently enhanced.

#### III. Final Judgment.

This stage is executed by the judge agent that possesses specialized
auxiliary diagnostic capabilities. Its major responsibility is to
integrate the feedback and make a scientifically sound decision. The
judge agent is capable of handling complex opinion conflicts, extracting
key arguments, and identifying areas of consensus and dispute. The judge
agent serves as a final reviewer in the medical image assessment,
synthesizing expert opinions and supporting the decision-making. In
detail, it analyzes the complete dialogue between the mediator agent and
the VLMs agent and organizes their core conclusions by extracting areas
of consensus and disagreement from these agents. Based on this analysis,
the judge agent combines the mediator agent’s focus to infer the
conclusion and make the final diagnostic judgment.

## 4 Experiments and Results

### 4.1 Experiment Settings

Benchmarks. We use five widely-adopted medical VQA benchmarks, including
VQA-RAD ([Lau et al. 2018](#bib.bib18)), SLAKE ([Liu et al.
2021](#bib.bib24)), PathVQA ([He et al. 2020](#bib.bib14)), PMC-VQA
([Zhang et al. 2023](#bib.bib45)), and a comprehensive benchmark
OmniMedVQA ([Hu et al. 2024](#bib.bib15)). VQA-RAD centers on
radiological images, and SLAKE encompasses a diverse range of medical
image knowledge-intensive QA tasks. PathVQA focuses on tissue-level
pathology-related images and questions. PMC-VQA is derived from PubMed
Central, comprising 2,000 human-annotated QA pairs. For OmniMedVQA, we
employ its publicly available subset including eight imaging modalities:
computed tomography (CT), dermatological images (Der), fundus
photography (FP), magnetic resonance imaging (MR), microscopic images
(Mic), optical coherence tomography (OCT), ultrasound (US), and X-ray
images. Detailed dataset statistics are provided in the Appendix
Section: Benchmark Statistics.

Details. We systematically evaluate the performance of the proposed
approach against multiple baseline methods in various settings. The
baseline single-agent models included Qwen2.5-VL-7B ([Bai et al.
2025](#bib.bib2)), HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B ([Chen et al. 2024](#bib.bib6)),
LLaVA-Med-7B ([Li et al. 2023a](#bib.bib20)), Qwen2.5-VL-32B ([Bai
et al. 2025](#bib.bib2)), HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B ([Chen et al.
2024](#bib.bib6)), and LLaVA-Next-34B ([Liu et al. 2023a](#bib.bib25)),
with LLaVA-Med and HuatuoGPT-Vision being specialized medical VLMs. In
addition, three major multi-agent strategies were compared: judgment
(our baseline), voting ([Wang et al. 2022](#bib.bib37)), and MoA ([Wang
et al. 2024](#bib.bib36)). The experiments utilize three agent
configurations and tested three distinct combinations: (1) a combination
of three 7B models, including Qwen2.5-VL-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B,
LLaVA-Med-7B, denoted symbol $`\blacklozenge`$, (2) a combination of
three $`\sim`$ 32B models, including Qwen2.5-VL-32B,
HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B, and LLaVA-Next-34B, denoted symbol $`\clubsuit`$,
and (3) a combination of HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, and
HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B, denoted symbol $`\spadesuit`$. For the traditional
medical VQA benchmarks, judgment, voting, and MoA strategies all use
three models of approximately 32B. For the OmniMedVQA dataset, the
multi-agent methods used three 7B models. By default, both the mediator
agent and judge agent are set to Qwen2.5-32B ([Yang et al.
2024](#bib.bib42)). Furthermore, we compare our approach with existing
state-of-the-art (SOTA) multi-agent methods, including Reconcile ([Chen,
Saha, and Bansal 2023](#bib.bib7)), AutoGen ([Wu et al.
2023b](#bib.bib40)), DyLAN ([Liu et al. 2023b](#bib.bib26)), and
MedAgents ([Tang et al. 2023](#bib.bib33)), with comparative results
sourced from the MDAgents ([Kim et al. 2024](#bib.bib16)). Since the
MDAgents method is in the few-shot setting while we are conducting
zero-shot, we do not compare with it. All open-source models are
executed on a server equipped with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, using the
LMdeploy ([Contributors 2023](#bib.bib10)) and vLLM ([Kwon et al.
2023](#bib.bib17)) frameworks for acceleration. In the experiment of
“Choice on LLM for mediator agents”, the API call for GPT-4o-mini incurs
a cost of \$2.02.

Evaluation. To ensure the consistency across agents when evaluating VLM
performance on medical VQA tasks, we implement several standard
processing steps. First, single-agent models are prompted using a
unified instruction: “provide the answer”. Notably, we avoid imposing a
rigid response format, such as requiring answers to be framed within
predefined labels (e.g., “A” or “B”). This design allows each model to
respond in its natural output style, thereby preserving the integrity of
its reasoning process for subsequent analysis and integration by the
mediator agent. Second, to extract structured answers from these
unstructured outputs, we employ LLaMA-3.1-Instruct-8B ([Grattafiori
et al. 2024](#bib.bib13)) as a parser. The parser standardizes model
responses into an `<answer> option </answer>` format, thereby improving
the consistency with the downstream processing. At the final answer
selection stage, inspired by the LVLM-eHub framework ([Xu et al.
2024](#bib.bib41)), we apply a semantic similarity matching between the
parsed answer and the original candidate options. The option with the
highest similarity score is selected as the final model’s prediction.
Accuracy is used as the evaluation metric in all experiments.

### 4.2 Experimental Results

Results on the widely-adopted medical VQA benchmarks. We systematically
evaluate the MedOrch on four medical VQA benchmarks, including VQA-RAD
([Lau et al. 2018](#bib.bib18)), SLAKE ([Liu et al. 2021](#bib.bib24)),
PathVQA ([He et al. 2020](#bib.bib14)), and PMC-VQA ([Lau et al.
2018](#bib.bib18)). We compare our method against both single-agent and
multi-agent methods. From Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ III. Final Judgment. ‣ 3.2 Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration ‣ 3 Method ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making"),
in the combination of small-scale models, ours^(⧫) (comprising three 7B
models) achieves an average accuracy of 63.38%, outperforming all
individual 7B models and multi-agent approaches. This demonstrates the
effectiveness of inter-model collaboration even on a relatively modest
scale.

On the larger scale, ours^(♣) (comprising three $`\sim`$32B models)
achieves the highest overall performance, with an average accuracy of
66.98%, attaining the leading scores on VQA-RAD (79.28%) and PMC-VQA
(50.50%). Compared to the best-performing single 32B model, this
configuration yielded a performance improvement ranging from +0.03% to
+19.52%, highlighting both the upper-bound performance potential of our
multi-agent system across diverse medical VQA scenarios. LLaVA-Next-34B
underperforms among the 32B models, achieving only 38.90% accuracy on
PMC-VQA, revealing its limited domain transferability in medical
contexts. Notably, our multi-agent system maintains strong performance
even when incorporating this weaker model, demonstrating resilience to
the underperforming agent. As our baseline, the judgment method does not
outperform the HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B in average performance. When
integrating with our multi-agent collaboration framework, we find that
the performance improves substantially (an average gain of 4.78%). Other
multi-agent methods exhibit higher sensitivity and generally fail to
outperform the strongest individual agents. For instance, MoA exhibits
strong performance on the PathVQA dataset but experiences a notable
decline on the more challenging PMC-VQA dataset.

To further investigate the effect of model robustness, we construct a
hybrid configuration ours^(♠) by replacing LLaVA-Next-34B with the
HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B model. This multi-agent framework achieved its best
performance on SLAKE (76.20%) and PathVQA (65.14%), with an overall
average accuracy of 66.96%. These results underscore the collaboration
value of diverse models within multi-agent systems.

We also report the performance gains relative to the weakest and best
individual models (↑Max/Min Gap). Overall, our performance improvement
is consistent across datasets given the design of our multi-agent
workflow. For instance, ours^(♣) outperforms the weakest model by
+15.39% on SLAKE and surpasses the best model by +4.33%. This confirms
that the proposed system can mitigate the limitations of weaker agents
and amplify the strength of stronger ones via the proposed multi-agent
collaboration system. A detailed case is shown in Appendix Section: Case
Study.

Results on the OmniMedVQA. We evaluate the proposed multi-agent
framework on OmniMedVQA, a large-scale medical VQA dataset that spans
eight imaging modalities. From Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making"),
ours^(⧫), comprising multiple 7B models, exhibits strong performance
among all evaluated approaches. It outperforms both multi-agent methods
and the best-performing individual models. In particular, for the FP and
Mic modalities, ours^(⧫) achieved substantial accuracy improvements of
+28.43% and +23.15%, respectively. These gains effectively compensated
for individual model deficiencies in certain modalities, highlighting
the framework’s capability to enhance modality-specific robustness. In
the more challenging modalities, such as OCT and US, individual models
like Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-Med-7B exhibit relatively poor performance.
Ours^(⧫) does not outperform the strong single models yet surpasses
other multi-agent methods, delivering notable improvements over the
weakest agents with gains of +15.46% and +23.20%, respectively. These
results demonstrate MedOrch’s strong ability to suppress the negative
influence of underperformed agents.

Comparison with GPT-4V based multi-agent methods. We further compare
MedOrch, fully based on open-source models, against both GPT-4V and
state-of-the-art multi-agent systems based on GPT-4V. As seen in Figure
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making"),
our method achieves an average accuracy of 64.8%, substantially
exceeding GPT-4V (57.9%) and other multi-agent counterparts on the
PathVQA dataset. In particular, we find that multi-agent methods ([Wu
et al. 2023b](#bib.bib40); [Liu et al. 2023b](#bib.bib26); [Tang et al.
2023](#bib.bib33)) originally designed for language tasks struggle to
perform well in multimodal scenarios. Their performance evidently falls
far behind the results achieved by using GPT-4V alone. In contrast, our
multi-agent method demonstrates greater adaptability, underscoring the
potential of an open-source compatible framework in medical multi-agent
intelligence.

Comparison with homogeneous multi-agent system. To evaluate the
performance of the multi-agent framework under a homogeneous model
configuration, we construct multiple agents using the same base model of
HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B. Specifically, we simulate three expert agents by
running three independent inference trials of the same model, each with
a temperature setting of 0.6 as seen in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making")
(a). Under such a setting, multi-agent framework is unable to leverage
the diversity across different models and thus we discourage the use of
identical models. In contrast, we construct a heterogeneous multi-agent
system composed of three different models towards performance gains.
Notably, the two additional models, Qwen2.5-VL-32B and LLaVA-Next-34B,
are weaker than HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B, as shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ III. Final Judgment. ‣ 3.2 Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration ‣ 3 Method ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making").
This shows that agents with complementary perspectives can collaborate
more effectively, even when some individual agents are less capable.
Thus, a heterogeneous multi-agent system combining different VLMs is
recommended.

Choice on LLM for mediator agents. We compare difference choices on LLM
for mediator agents, including GPT-4o-mini (whose API fee is affordable)
and Qwen2.5-32B. The results of PathVQA and PMC-VQA datasets are shown
in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making")
(b). Qwen2.5-32B achieves relatively high performance, with the accuracy
of 64.8% and 50.5% in respective dataset. GPT-4o-mini shows a
significant drop in performance, resulting in a lower overall accuracy.
Note that we have explored the feasibility of using smaller models by
evaluating a 7B-scale LLM as the mediator. However, we find that such
small-scale models struggle to follow complex instructions and
frequently fail to complete the tasks. Overall, these results highlight
the value of using open-source LLMs with a proper scale for the mediator
agent role in the multi-agent VQA system.

![Refer to caption](2508.05996v2/Figures/two_agents.png)

Figure 4: Evidence of collaborative synergy in MedOrch on PathVQA

Choice on LLM for judge agents. To investigate the impact of judge agent
on the performance, we compare the variants of the Qwen-2.5 series with
7B and 32B parameters, as summarized in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Mediator-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration among Open-Source Models for Medical Decision-Making")
(c). The small-scale model, Qwen-2.5-7B, exhibits suboptimal
performance, achieving the accuracy of 62.0% on PathVQA and only 43.35%
on PMC-VQA. It indicates small-scale model has limited capacity for
handling complex medical dialogues. Scaling up to 32B results in a
substantial performance gain, achieving an accuracy of 64.8% on PathVQA
and 50.50% on PMC-VQA. These findings underscore the effectiveness of
models in semantic understanding and information integration.
Qwen2.5-32B model offers a more favorable configuration for both
mediator and judge agents, making it well-suited for deployment in
practical applications.

“Conformity effect” or collaborative synergy? We investigate whether the
performance improvements observed during the collaboration stage are
genuinely due to effective cooperation, or merely a result of the
“conformity effect”. “The conformity effect” refers to the tendency of
individuals within a group to align with the majority opinion during the
collaborative discussion.

To test this hypothesis, we introduce a two-agent configuration using
HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B and LLaVA-Next-34B. In this two-agent setting, the
possibility of “minority yielding to majority” is strictly eliminated,
making it a suitable setup to assess the effect of true collaborative
synergy. Notably, we observe that performance improves even in this
restricted two-agent setup, where the accuracy increases from 62.61%
(HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B alone) to 64.32% with collaboration. This is
particularly compelling given that LLaVA-Next-34B alone achieves only
53.76% that is lower than HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B. When combined under our
proposed framework, the result demonstrates an effect of multi-agent
collaboration. These findings strongly suggest that the observed
performance gains are not simply the result of conformity during group
decision-making. Instead, they point to genuine complementarity and
effective collaboration between heterogeneous agents.

### 4.3 Discussion and Limitation

Designing a collaborative system to handle multimodal clinical data is
challenging given the complex healthcare workflow ([Tu et al.
2024](#bib.bib35); [Acosta et al. 2022](#bib.bib1)). We explore the
multi-agent collaboration from a collaboration perspective and measure
its communication stability. In particular, our approach consistently
outperformed the strongest single agent across diverse setups, including
expert agent scale, composition, and mediator type. Towards a stable
coordination mechanism, our approach leverages structured outputs
generated by the mediator LLM and employs an automated
regular-expression-based parsing to ensure a high coordination
reliability. This setting strongly differs from AFlow ([Zhang et al.
2024b](#bib.bib44)) that relies on search-based interactions yet suffers
from its instability. Crucially, our findings reveal that heterogeneous
multi-agent systems are particularly well-suited for leveraging
open-source models in clinical applications.

Multi-agent frameworks inevitably introduce longer inference times
compared to single-agent systems, primarily due to coordination overhead
([Cheng et al. 2024](#bib.bib9)). In our design, the main source of
increased inference time stems from the collaborative stage. To reduce
this, the mediator agent queries each expert agent only once without
repeating the interaction process. In addition, we generate all
questions of the mediator agent in a single forward pass and run
multiple expert agents in parallel to handle responses. This yields an
overall inference time approximately twice that of a single-agent
system. We view this as a reasonable trade-off given the performance
gains and believe the gap will further narrow with more optimizations of
inference systems ([Kwon et al. 2023](#bib.bib17); [Contributors
2023](#bib.bib10)).

Our approach relies entirely on the agents’ internal capabilities
without the retrieval-augmented generation ([Lewis et al.
2020](#bib.bib19)) and tools ([Cheng et al. 2024](#bib.bib9)).
Incorporating real-world clinical data or medical knowledge can further
enhance the system’s performance in structured clinical workflows. Using
specialized tools, such as imaging diagnostics and report generation,
could advance the multi-agent collaboration and interpretable
decision-making in the healthcare system.

## 5 Conclusion

We propose MedOrch as a collaborative framework and verify that
open-source multimodal agents can develop effective collaboration
strategies for clinical decision-making. MedOrch builds upon the joint
strength of open-source expert agents under the guidance of an LLM
mediator agent. MedOrch enhances collaboration and addresses conflict
resolution in complex medical conversations, such as error propagation
and constrained inferential depth derived from individual VLMs.
Comprehensive evaluations across five benchmark datasets demonstrate
that our method attains strong performance without additional training.
These findings underscore the potential of a reflective mediator-guided
collaboration in enhancing medical multimodal intelligence.

## Prompts

The following set of prompts constitutes a comprehensive multi-agent
decision-making framework tailored for medical multimodal multi-agent
collaboration. Each prompt plays a specialized role in ensuring
rigorous, iterative, and collaborative evaluation and answer generation.
Together, they facilitate an efficient pipeline from initial answer
synthesis to final decision-making. The prompts are summarized as
follows:

Prompt to mediator agent for Socratic Questioning. This prompt is
designed for the mediator agent, who acts as the final authority in
medical decision-making. It evaluates the initial opinions from a group
of experts, determines whether further discussion is necessary, and, if
so, conducts structured Socratic-style dialogues with each expert.

Prompt for Feedback-based Answering. This prompt is intended for expert
agents and focuses on refinement in response to questions posed by the
mediator agent.

Prompt for Final Judgment. This prompt is designed for the judge agent
for final judgment. It deeply analyzes complex multi-party discussions,
and infers the most likely final decision.

Prompt for Answer Refinement. This prompt is used during evaluation
stage. An LLM extracts structured answers from unstructured model
outputs, ensuring that the format is consistent across evaluations of
different vision-language models.
